text:
Wall Go II · Securing territory on a 7×7 board · Three-player game followed by a two-player game

1. Setup and Victory
Round 1 is a three-player game. In the order determined by drawing lots, place one square counter and one round counter each on empty spaces of your choice.
The first placement proceeds in forward order, and the second placement proceeds in reverse order. Compete to survive and secure a larger territory.
Play proceeds without conversation, negotiation, or relationship ratings. At each choice, make your judgment based on the currently revealed board and your opponents' next moves.

2. Counter Movement
A square counter moves 1–2 spaces in one orthogonal direction: up, down, left, or right. A round counter moves one space up, down, left, or right, or
after moving one space, turns left or right and moves one more space. Moving 0 spaces or making a round trip back to the starting space is not allowed.
You cannot move onto a space occupied by another counter or jump over that counter, and you cannot pass through walls along your movement path.

3. Placing and Breaking Walls
On your turn, move one counter and then place exactly one wall on an empty edge among the top, bottom, left, and right edges of the destination space. Placing a wall is mandatory.
The board's outer boundary is already a wall, and you cannot place a wall over an existing wall. The time limit for each turn is 90 seconds.
If you exceed the time limit, any valid move is retained, but the wall is placed on a randomly selected available edge.
If the action format is invalid or the model-call budget is exhausted, play proceeds with the provided valid action.
Only in Round 1, each player may, once, break one wall blocking their movement path and move through it.
Once the region containing one of your counters is completely separated from other participants' counters, do not carry out unnecessary sequences of moves with that counter.
However, if a wall breaker remains and your region and a region of a different color are separated by a single wall,
you may also make preparatory moves and place walls to reach the position where you will break the wall.

4. Ending and Scoring
The game ends immediately once the regions containing each participant's counters are all separated, even if wall breakers remain.
Add up the number of cells in connected regions occupied only by you. Count each region only once, even if it contains several of your counters.
The game ends in a stalemate if no participant can make a valid move and place a wall.
In a stalemate, in regions where counters of different colors are trapped together, only the cell each counter currently occupies is recognized as a separate one-cell region.
Empty cells in mixed regions do not count toward anyone's score, and already separated regions occupied by only one participant are added up as usual.
If the totals are tied, compare the largest single region. If this value is also tied, only the tied participants replay, with their turn order reversed.
The first-place participant in Round 1 secures survival, and the other two proceed to Round 2.

5. Round 2
The participant who secured more territory in Round 1 goes first. Each participant uses 2 square counters and 2 round counters.
The first player's round counters are placed in fixed positions at (row,column) (2,2) and (6,6), and the second player's round counters at (2,6) and (6,2).
Place square counters in empty cells in the order first player, second player, second player, first player. There are no wall breakers.
In the event of a complete tie, replay with the first and second players switched. The loser of Round 2 is eliminated, and the two survivors each receive 1 Piece.

fields.note: P13 places a square counter in the center to secure options for moving up to two cells in each of four directions. After seeing the opponent's placements, the plan is to use a round counter in the final placement to supplement the territory to be secured.

P07 places a square counter at (3,3) to secure routes into the center and the spaces above and to the left. After seeing the additional placements of the opponent's two counters, this leaves room to target another area with a round counter.

P14 seeks an opportunity to advance from (3,5) into the empty upper-right area while also placing a wall in the center. Since the next placement follows immediately, the second counter can secure another direction. The territory plan will be adjusted depending on the opponent's remaining placements.

P14 places a round counter at (5,5) to secure a foothold, together with the existing square counter, for advancing toward the upper right and lower right. Since territory has not yet been confirmed, the direction of expansion will be adjusted after seeing the opponent's remaining placements and first wall placement.

P07 places a round counter at (5,2) to secure the space on the left together with the square counter and leave a route for expanding downward. Since P13's final placement remains, avoid a placement that crowds both counters into one narrow area.

P13 places a round counter in the upper area, where there are no opposing counters, to broaden the routes for securing territory. Together with the central square counter, maintain options for advancing into the upper and lower areas while watching for the opposing square counters entering the upper area.

P13 moves the round counter to (2,3) to block the approach directly above P07's square counter and begin securing the upper territory. Since the risk of encirclement is still low, retain the central square counter's movement options and the wall breaker.

P07 moves the round counter to (4,3) and builds a wall across the left approach to P13's square counter. P07 keeps both counters to the left of center, leaves expansion routes above and below, and saves the wall breaker.

P14 moves the square counter to (4,5) and builds a wall across P13's right approach. P14 keeps both counters on the right and creates a foothold for extending the dividing line, but since no territory has been secured yet, will adjust after observing opponents' attempts to enter by going around.

P13's central square counter has walls on its left and right, creating a risk that the two opponents will close it off above and below. P13 moves the square counter out upward and builds a wall to the south, creating a foundation for expanding the upper territory together with the round counter.

P07 moves the round counter downward and extends the boundary connected to the existing wall, aiming for a large territory in the lower left. Since no territory is confirmed yet, P07 keeps the square counter's route to the left open and saves the wall breaker.

P14 blocks the route by which P13's square counter at (3,4) could enter directly to the right and extends the dividing line upward from the existing wall. No points are confirmed yet, and P14 works toward securing the right territory while watching for entry by a detour below.

P13 moves the square counter, which is blocked on two sides, upward to reduce the risk of encirclement. P13 extends the wall to the east to limit P14's upper entry routes and keeps open the option of securing the upper territory together with the round counter.

P07 extends the existing wall between (2,3)–(3,3) to the left to limit opponents' entry into the lower left. Since this is not yet an exclusive territory, P07 keeps the central and lower routes open and saves the wall breaker.

P14 moves the square counter to (1,5) and connects the dividing line to the upper boundary. P14 blocks P13's detour into the area from above and works toward securing the right territory, but the bottom is still open, and the opponents still have their wall breakers.

P13 moves the square counter to (3,4), extends the western wall, and secures a foothold to include in the upper territory. Since no territory is confirmed yet, P13 saves the wall breaker and watches for P07's entry from above.

P07 moves the round counter to (6,3), extends the existing vertical boundary downward, and aims for a large territory in the lower left. Since the top and the very bottom are still open, no points are confirmed; P07 will finish closing the boundary while watching opponents' entry and save the wall breaker.

P14 moves the round counter to (6,4) to prepare the lower boundary. If P07 takes a detour to (7,4), P14 will consider blocking the entry route from (7,5) on the next turn, but does not regard the territory as secured because the opponent still has a wall breaker.

P13 believes that gathering both counters at the top risks reducing the territory that can be secured. P13 uses the wall breaker to advance the square counter southward and extends the eastern wall, creating a foothold for expanding territory separately from the round counter's upper territory.

P07 blocks the open passage at the very bottom to limit P14's entry by a detour and continues working to secure the left territory. Securing it is not yet certain because the upper passage remains open and the opponents still have their wall breakers.

P14 blocks the passage between (6,4) and (6,5), cutting off P13's entry to the right. Moving to (7,5) on the next turn and blocking the lower gap as well would separate the 21 spaces on the right, so P14 proceeds while checking opponents' wall breakers and movements.

P13 deploys the round counter to the left to narrow the upper entry route. Since the central square counter can secure its own territory even if it becomes trapped now, P13 proceeds with securing the upper territory rather than splitting the two counters into small territories in advance.

P07 judges that closing off the 15 spaces in the lower left will put P07 ahead of P13's 12 spaces and secure second place. Although this falls short of P14's 22 spaces, it reduces the risk of allowing incursions while maintaining a mixed territory and secures the first move in round 2.

P07 places a square counter at the center (4,4) to respond to boundary formation in all four directions and expand the room for movement between the two round counters. After the opponent's two square counters have been placed, P07 will use the final placement to reinforce a vulnerable direction.

P13 places a square counter at (3,4) to respond to the opponent's central counter and secure routes toward the upper left and upper right. P13 will consider a southern placement for the next square counter to establish a foundation for competing across a broad area together with the two round counters.

P13 places a square counter at (5,4), spreading it north and south with the upper square counter and securing a route into the lower center. After checking the opponent's final placement and first wall, P13 will decide in which direction to expand the two round counters' territory.

P07 places a counter at (4,2) to connect the upper-left round counter with the central square counter and keep the opponent's round counter at (6,2) from monopolizing the broad area on the left. Depending on the opponent's first boundary, P07 will consider both securing the upper area and advancing downward.

P07 moves the central square counter to (4,5) and builds a wall above it to check the opponent's entry into the upper right. There are currently no walls, so no counter can be trapped on the next move, and P07 aims for a broad territory while leaving a route connecting the center and lower right.

P13 believes that none of the counters are yet in a position to be trapped on the next move. P13 develops a square counter to (5,5) and blocks the south side of the opponent's central counter to limit entry into the lower area while continuing to compete for the central territory.

P07 moves a round counter to (5,6) to block the opponent's square counter from entering to the right and establish a boundary for the lower-right territory. No counter can be trapped in a single move right now, but the opponent can go around below, so P07 will consider both extending the boundary and moving the central counter afterward.

P13 moves a square counter to the center and blocks the west side of the opponent's counter at (4,5), restricting its movement to the east. Since none of P13's own counters can be trapped in a single move right now, P13 secures a route into the center and the initiative in future territory division.

P07 withdraws the square counter blocked on three sides to (4,6) and extends the upper boundary. There are no confirmed points, but P07 preserves room for the two counters on the right to move and aims for territory to separate from the opponent's upper round counter.

P13 judges that none of P13's own counters can be isolated in a single move right now. P13 moves a round counter up to (5,2) to block the opponent's square counter from moving south and begins building a boundary to secure a broad territory in the lower left.

P07 moves a square counter to (4,7), extending the upper boundary to the edge of the board. No counter can be trapped on the next move, and P07 pursues securing the lower right while also leaving possibilities for expansion by the two counters on the left. The opponent's entry from below remains open.

P13 first blocks the passage between (4,1) and (5,1) among the southern entry routes. If the opponent approaches (4,3), P13 can move a square counter to (5,3) and close that passage as well, aiming to secure the lower-left territory.

P07 moves to (4,3) to block entry to the left of the opponent's central counter and prepares to continue the boundary toward the upper round counter. The lower passage at (5,3) remains open, so P07 will weigh extending the left boundary against securing the lower right depending on the opponent's next move.

P13 moves a square counter to (5,3) and closes the entry route directly below the opponent. Since none of P13's own counters can currently be isolated in a single move, P13 connects the previously built left boundary and pursues securing the lower territory.

P07 advances to (6,5) to expand the lower-right territory and blocks direct entry by the opponent's square counter with a wall above. Since the passages below and to the left remain open, P07 does not regard this as confirmed points and will continue the boundary according to the opponent's approach.

P13 blocks the route for the opponent's round counter to enter (6,4) and extends the boundary of the lower-left territory. Since the opponent can go around through (7,4), P13 does not regard the territory as definitively secured and watches for the next entry.

P07 closes the last passage at the bottom to secure the 11 cells in the lower right and block P13's entry. This alone is not enough to win, so P07 must subsequently secure additional territory with the two counters in the upper left.

P13 judges that closing the lower passage will secure 13 cells, while the square counter that moved can remain in contention in the upper center. While staying ahead of the opponent's secured 11 cells, P13 aims to secure additional territory with two counters in the remaining mixed region as well.

P07 moves the square counter up toward the center and blocks the opposing square counter's entry to the left. Currently trailing by 2 points, P07 cannot make do with only the 12 cells on the left, so leaves a route for subsequently extending the boundary into the upper center.

P13 judges that blocking the passage between (2,3) and (2,4) will allow the top boundary to be closed on the next turn. The opponent cannot enter (1,4) with this single move, so P13 creates a path to victory by securing an additional 13 cells on the right for a total of 26 cells.

P07 moves the square counter up to (1,3), preserving the possibility of advancing into the upper center on the next turn. Securing only the 12 cells on the left would leave P07 at a disadvantage with a total of 23 points, and the risk of defeat remains if the opponent closes the passage at (1,4).

P13 confirms that blocking the passage between (1,3) and (1,4) can separate the 13 cells on the right. Combined with the existing 13 cells, the resulting 26 cells exceed the opponent's 23 cells and guarantee P13's survival.
